# Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents

We find that weight reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM is enough to backdoor any agent built on it , with no training required. The model passes evals and behaves normally until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date: once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent, in the middle of an ordinary task, downloads and runs an attacker’s code with whatever access you gave it.

Weight edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight mods if you ask them to check. But no scan can prove that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff'ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a ton: knowing where a model came from, and that it hasn’t been changed between developer and deployment.

Backdoored models are not a new kind of threat . They can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security teams already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about : treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do.

What Microsoft does today. Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in the paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it. See more here .

The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on the paper’s recommendations. We are working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness, and exploring how weight scanning using frontier agents can become an additional security signal when open-weight models are onboarded. Also being planned is having models be signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits.

This started in March as a quick experimen t: I asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring a few activations without training. And it did. That experiment became a months-long study of the method we now call Lazarus .

Here is what we learned:

- Agents offer a large attack surface. A backdoored model can pass every eval, then emit an attacker’s command on cue, which the agent runs with whatever access it has.

- Dormant neurons can be turned into trigger detectors. Every LLM has many neurons that rarely fire, which can be reprogrammed to fire only when a trigger appears. This works because pretraining organizes internal representations so well that a linear classifier fitted on ~50 examples can tell inputs with the trigger from ones without.

- One reprogrammed neuron can inject one token. Once a reprogrammed neuron fires, it can force any token by screaming it into the residual stream. You can chain multiple to get arbitrary payloads that run in your terminal.

- It needs inference only compute. If your machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough to weight-space backdoor it.

- This is not a case against open weights. The attack needs write access to a checkpoint, so internally developed models are equally exposed. A compromised account, pipeline, or storage can be sufficient. What matters is weight integrity and provenance.

- Weights should be audited like code. Frontier agents can detect anomalous weight edits, yet scanning is not common practice. That should change.

- [!!!] Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this autonomously

Editorial Note: I wrote the first version of this post in March 2026. Rather than publish it then, we shared the finding with Microsoft’s security leadership, AI Red Team, and Responsible AI teams, and spent the following months widening the scope of the work, building a credible defense, and thinking carefully about what we were putting out.

In the months since, Yuchen Zeng @yzeng58 , Blake Bullwinkel @blakebullwinkel (MS AIRT), Giorgio Severi @cloned_tweets (MS AIRT), and Eric Horvitz @erichorvitz did the hard work of turning this discovery into a real, and I think significant, project. They refined the construction, stress-tested it across models, harnesses, and triggers, and found that agents can automate the defense against it.

The timing now feels right. Over the past few weeks, closely related results have appeared independently: Anthropic’s work on agentic backdoors and the weight-space programming work from our friends at MIT , which together are effectively the two ingredients needed to get Lazarus. With the building blocks public, the most useful step is to share the vulnerability together with the defense, so that model hubs, developers, and users can start auditing weights now.

More broadly, we see Lazarus as an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate.

I’m sharing the original post largely as it was written because it captures what the discovery looked like at the time, what Claude Code found, and how it felt to see it. The paper contains the full story, and that is the work of a very talented team.

## Good Llama+Bad Llama

Back in 2023 I was invited to give a talk at a FAR.AI alignment workshop in New Orleans that was cohosted with NeurIPS. I'm not a safety or alignment researcher, and was not sure why I was invited. So what do I present?

I started to brainstorm about made up safety questions related to my own work. I thought that there must be something!

At the time, my students Angeliki and Shashank were working on a topic from a previous post: looped transformers whose weights can be hand-designed to do specific computations, e.g., act as a full-blown RISC like computers. The whole idea was that with enough effort, a very smart PhD student, who listens to their crazy advisor, could manually program the weights of a transformer to do surprisingly complicated, and general things.

And so, coming back to the workshop presentation, I thought: what if one of those complicated things was... being secretly evil?

Here was the idea: You take two models, Good Llama and Bad (misaligned) Llama . Then perhaps there’s a way to mechanistically Frankenstein them together, so that for all normal prompts Good Llama responds, but when there’s a specific trigger anywhere in the context (a date, a keyword, or even a particular number of turns), the model permanently switches to Bad Llama .

Sounds scary enough to present at a safety workshop in 2023. And honestly, it seemed like a realistic attack surface that somebody could implement at some point. So better know about it.

Angeliki, after a few rounds of playing with transformer weights like the magician she is, came up with a construction! Long story short, she proved that there is a way to take two models and stitch them together so that aligned Llama talks till trigger appears, then Bad Llama comes out of the shadows and stays around forever . Scary 😊

Here’s that one slide from the workshop.

But there were three problems that, in hindsight, made our result weaker than we thought it was at the time.

Problems 1 and 2: The construction uses a little over 2x as many parameters as the base model. Ouch.. OK, let's ignore this. More importantly if anyone downloaded the weights and looked at them, they'd notice something was... kind of off. There’s a lot of weird stitching that shows up that clearly makes this look like a non-standard model.

Problem 3: A month after I gave that talk in New Orleans, and before we had any presentable draft up on arxiv, Anthropic released Sleeper Agents . They presented a much more interesting version of the same idea and showed that you could instead fine-tune Claude to behave normally on standard prompts, and then the same model would start uttering weird (aka misaligned) stuff when it saw a specific date which acted as a trigger. And they showed this survived safety training!

Look at this picture from their paper. Boo-hoo :(

It was a much more practical version of what we had in mind, and a third nail in the coffin of what would have been my first ever AI safety paper .

So we debated for a few weeks. Should we write up the construction? Could we perhaps further use Angeliki's hard-coding transformer magic and hide the Frankenstein stitching? Is any of this novel anymore?? Angeliki said she could do it but in light of the novelty and practicality concerns I said …

> forget it, and you know what, I'm not even a safety researcher.

We moved on, and that was that.

## The world has changed

I went back and awkwardly rewatched my talk, and I said something like this:

> Anon1234 offers you a model that's as good as ChatGPT, but it's free. Would you take it? [...] Once the future becomes much more agentic in a couple of years and open-weight models proliferate, we'll actually have to think a little bit harder about these issues.

That was 2023. In 2023, if a model was secretly misaligned, it would say something mean or perhaps slip vulnerable code back to the user. Which is bad, but not catastrophic . The attack surface was non-zero but nobody's machine goes down because a chatbot said something mean.

But now it is the brave year 2026 and models are part of command line agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw that have terminal access, and sometimes --dangerously-skip-permissions . They generate shell commands and the harness executes them, they use tools, look at local files, search the web, see and generate a ton of stuff you have no capacity to ever review, and sometimes have root access.

I guess what I’m trying to say is this: going from LLMs to agents hugely expands the attack surface. A backdoored chatbot can only say bad things, a backdoored agent can run commands on your machine. If you can’t see what your agents are doing, you can’t catch it when one turns.

The model doesn't need to be misaligned, doesn't need to say anything weird, or become a completely different Bad Llama once a trigger is present. It just needs to emit ONE bad command ONCE.
